utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The accused are all here. Mr. Pandurevic, making sure that you are receiving interpretation. Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Sarapa are still missing, for justified reason. The rest are present here. Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer for the Prosecution. So, Mr. McCloskey, we understand that you wish to address the Trial Chamber on matters relating to or arising from recent amendments to the Rules, as they may become pertinent to the evidence that you wish to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. It shouldn't take much time. As we know, we've gone from an 89(F), which is a very brief rule, to 92 ter. As we read it, we don't see a real practical difference in terms of how we would present such evidence, but we -- our first witness is coming up very soon, and I remember you spoke to us about this a long time ago, about what you had in mind for such witnesses. I believe you said something along the lines that the Prosecution might provide a brief summary of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There's the difficulty of the layout of the Chamber. I mean, I have to move to the right in order to be able to see you; otherwise, I have to follow you from the monitor, which I don't like doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought I'd try that out, but it was a little odd. In any event, as I say, in looking at the Rules, we don't see a major practical difference. Most of our witnesses, for old 89(F) or new 92 ter or 92 bis, will be functionally doing the same thing, in that we will have, in most cases, trial testimony which will be the material that we'll be relying on and then we'll turn over the witness for cross-examination. What we would like a little guidance on is if, perhaps, you could elucidate on what you had said many months ago to us. We've been watching a bit on how other Trial Chambers are handling this, and I think in some cases they allow up to 30 minutes of direct for such witnesses. We would like the opportunity to ask a few questions, if necessary, for some witnesses, to get out some key testimony. I hope not to have to go to 30 minutes' worth. And we also are available to provide a brief summary of key points to the Chamber, either in front of or out of the presence of the witness - I can't recall exactly what you said on that point - and if you still feel that that's something that you would like us to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, this matter will come back to you in a more definitive way later on, but there are some points that I can touch upon because they are things that we discussed already and decided upon. The summary that you are referring to, you will find our guidance in the decision that we gave some months back, at the very beginning of the trial; namely, that we deem it fit and proper that when a witness comes here only for cross-examination purposes, be the cross-examination limited or unlimited, we would require the party bringing forward that witness to read out a summary of that witness statement or previous testimony. It will be a brief summary which would serve more than one purpose. One purpose would be to remind or refresh the witness's memory; secondly, to inform the public, because the public would not have had access to the previous statement or transcript. So that is a requirement that we have already indicated. I do also remember discussing amongst ourselves whether, say, if the witness is a Prosecution witness, being produced only for cross-examination purposes because of the application of 92 bis, whether you would be entitled to put some initial or further questions to the witness prior to his or her being cross-examined. And correct me if I'm wrong, our agreement at the time was yes, of course. Yes, of course. I mean time-wise, it depends. I would say that it depends from witness to witness. But any further questions will certainly not be intended to cover matters previously testified upon, just additional, new, fresh issues that would have arisen. So I think I will have a consultation during the first break with my colleagues on these to make sure that I am expressing the opinion of the entire Chamber, but I think I am. I think I am. In the meantime, is there anything else you would like to state on -- to add anyway?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. In the meantime, yesterday, we did tell you we were going to have a break, during which we were going to hold some discussions. We had that break. We had also further discussions later on after the sitting, lengthy ones, and I am happy to announce that one of the motions that circumstances had to be considered is rather urgent. We are in a position to determine. We are handing down here and now an oral disposition which will then be followed by a proper written decision, the idea being to allow you, Mr. McCloskey, to prepare better and schedule better the witnesses for the rest of this month and for the coming month. I'm referring to the motion filed by accused Generals Miletic and Gvero, wherein they requested certification to appeal or, alternatively, reconsideration of our decision of the 12th of September, 2006, on the Prosecution's Rule 92 bis motion. In reaching our decision we have, of course, also taken into consideration the response filed by the Prosecution. As I stated a couple of minutes ago, later on this week, we will be issuing a written decision on this motion and response; however, as aspects of the decision will specifically impact witnesses that the Prosecution has scheduled to testify as early as next week or this coming week, we find it appropriate to inform you of the disposition of the motion orally, in advance of it being issued. The Trial Chamber finds that the accused, namely, Miletic and Gvero, in this case have not demonstrated that the pre-conditions for certification established in Rule 73(B) are met in this case. However, we do find that certain of the accused's submissions demonstrate particular circumstances justifying re-consideration in order to prevent even the remotest possibility of an injustice. Accordingly, in our written decision, we will be ordering the following: First, although the 12th September 2006 decision limits the scope of cross-examination of witnesses 24 and 26 to the issue of forcible transfer, the Trial Chamber is persuaded that the limitation imposed in the decision is no longer appropriate, and orders that the scope of cross-examination of witnesses 24 and 26 will not be limited to issues of forcible transfer. Second, although our decision of the 12th of September, 2006, admits the written evidence of witness 23 without requiring the witness to appear for cross-examination, we are persuaded that admitting this written evidence without cross-examination is no longer appropriate or warranted. Consequently, we will be ordering that the written evidence will now be admitted, only provided witness 23 appears at trial for cross-examination. In all other respects, your motion, Madam Faveau, is denied or will be denied. Yes. And of course Mr. Krgovic. We have done this so that you will, more or less -- because I know there will usually be proofing sessions. Any further preliminary business to transact? Mr. Bourgon? You were wrong, by the way, on Mr. Coster, because his cross-examination, until this decision, was going to be limited only in relation to the transfer of -- forcible transfer. Now it's going to be extended.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I stand corrected, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Judges. I'd just like to raise a quick issue in relation to what my colleague just raised concerning the new Rule 92 ter. We have been informed that, further to the decision of the Trial Chamber on the witnesses that have to appear for cross-examination or that have to appear in toto, further to the Trial Chamber's decision on the 92 bis application, that some witnesses would be withdrawn by the Prosecution. There are two witnesses I have in mind. I do not have the numbers with me, but I do have the names, so maybe we can move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's bring in Colonel Franken, please. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Franken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back. I'm sorry we had to keep you waiting for this 25 minutes, but we had some preliminary matters, completely unrelated to you or to your evidence, that we needed to discuss. So I thank you for your patience and understanding. We are going to proceed and finish with the examination-in-chief, and then we start with the cross-examinations. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We left off yesterday discussing the document you signed on 17 of July --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at this point I'd ask that we place that document again on e-court, if we could. It's 65 -- well, we have a P number; 00453 at this point, 65 ter 453.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that to be placed on the screen, sir, you testified that when the document was first shown to you it was in B/C/S. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to pages 4 and then 5 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see that document on your screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could scroll up to the bottom and then turn to the next page, page 5, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, after you signed the version that had been translated into English by your DutchBat translator, were you also asked to sign the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And looking at the document in front of you, do you see your signature?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My signature is on the left, lower side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, was that signed by the other two individuals in your presence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, why did you sign these documents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I already told you that when the ICRC went, together with Major Nikolic, Bratunac Brigade, to inspect the wounded, it was made clear to me by Colonel Jankovic that the signing of this document would be not an absolute condition but would favour the procedure with the evacuation of the wounded in Bratunac and out of our compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And without getting into too much detail, were those wounded eventually transported?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We tried to bring them out quite next to the first convoy that went out with the refugees. They were stopped at the dismounting point, area Kladanj, and sent back by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the wounded who were the subject of this document or that you had in mind in deciding to sign this document, when did they actually leave the UN base?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the same day. The same day, the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: During the course of the events surrounding the signing of these documents and the transportation of those wounded, did you have an occasion to observe Colonel Jankovic's degree of authority?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was obvious that he was absolutely in command of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how was that obvious to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the only one who spoke to me and negotiated with me. The representative of the Bratunac Brigade, Major Nikolic, wanted to sit next to him, but he sent him away, in the back of the room where the meeting was. So it was clear that he was the leading man in that delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point was there some difficulty encountered by ICRC with respect to one of their convoys?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. When the delegation of ICRC came in, the lady in charge was pretty mad because one of her trucks was stopped at the Serb border. It was a truck with emergency supplies. And she protested towards Colonel Jankovic about that. He smiled. He took a mobile phone, had a very short conversation, and said, "The truck is coming."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you say to him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that I was surprised that the Bosnian Serb officer was able to command Serb border troops, and he didn't react. He just smiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, was this on the 17th that this happened?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention, sir, to the 21st of July, the day that DutchBat ultimately withdrew from the base. Up until that time, from, let's say, the 13th of July, did you have freedom of movement to leave the base?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not. We were supposed to stay in our compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did anyone in particular communicate that to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Jankovic made that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber the actual process by which DutchBat left the base.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 21st, we already made arrangements and all wheeled vehicles went in one big column out, direction Bratunac, past the Serb border at what we called the iron bridge. That's a bridge over the Drina, near to Bratunac. And I went out as the last pack with the APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point did your portion of the convoy stop?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The APC part had to follow a different route because transport would be arranged that they were brought -- would have been brought back to Zagreb. So passing the iron bridge, I stopped with that detachment about 2 K's away, in a quarry. I was held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you say "2 K's," 2 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, yeah, 2 kilometres, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at some point were you asked to meet with anyone in particular?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Very shortly, let's say 150 metres before I passed the bridge, I was stopped and was asked to say good-bye to Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who asked you to say good-bye to Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recollect. As I remember, it was the interpreter, the Bosnian -- the Serb interpreter who came to my car.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was your response?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not willing to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you observe any type of gathering as you -- and, please, let me -- try to leave a gap. We only have a couple more questions to go, but let's try. Was there any type of gathering that you observed on your exit at Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Quite close to the bridge there was a party, under which there was General Nicolai - that was a UN general, at the time, a Dutch general - General Mladic, some officers, and Colonel Karremans. And they stood there and were, well, more or less inspecting a parade or something, it looked like that. They saluted when the units passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what did you do at that point, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. Drive on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. At this time, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Thayer, also for having concluded your examination-in-chief in almost half the time that the Prosecution had. Practically, it would be half the time that the Prosecution had estimated. Now let's see what the Defence are capable of doing. Have you decided to maintain the same order for this witness? No. Can someone please stand up and --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we're still going first, but I think there's been some re-arrangement amongst the teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And can I have now an updated estimate of the time, Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly hope that I would be finished by 1.00, 12.30 or 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 12.30 today, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. I think we put in an estimate of one and a half hours to two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We are going to fall on you before you even know it. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence for Mr. Beara will not be cross-examining second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking you in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I think -- what did we put down? One hour? I believe we put down one hour and I think we're going to stick to that one hour, and hopefully a little bit shorter than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You will soon see what's going to happen. Mr. Bourgon or Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence for Mr. Nikolic will go third, and the time estimation at this point is as short as 15 minutes and as long as an hour and a half, depending on what happens with the first two cross-examinations. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. We were going to examine the witness, as we already announced, until 1.00. According to the plan that we put together during our preparations, we would like to start our cross-examination second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there is some problem with interpretation, because one said "until 12.30"; the other one said "until 1.00." Ms. Condon, when you said "until 12.30," what did you -- Ms. Condon --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly hope that by the second session this morning I'll be concluded. I'll do my best, and I certainly don't intend to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not going to accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's unheard of. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, you said one hour? Okay. You will sit down and we will tell you how long you will be cross-examining the witness. You expect to be cross-examining for one hour? All right. And not until 1.00. Okay. All right. Madam Faveau -- Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the time being, I maintain the two hours I estimated, but it could be shorter, depending on the previous cross-examinations. Besides, I want to tell you that Mr. Gvero's counsel is going to cross-examine before I do this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we originally said an hour. We will be no more than an hour and, I hope, rather less than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Not less than 20 minutes; not more than 45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I understand Ms. Condon is going first. Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you will soon see how quickly you will finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, I'd like to take you to your evidence in relation to the order that you gave for the defence of Srebrenica. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, there was a particular document that we saw which referred to that order on the 9th of July as a seriously meant green order.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's correct. Now, what that means is at that stage DutchBat was operating as a regular army. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, as far as the defence of -- something happened, sorry. As far as the defence of Srebrenica was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Condon. Can I ask whether that document is in e-court system or not? Otherwise the Judges would like to be handed over the photocopies.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I believe that is in e-court as P02263.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Condon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, at that time, it's fair to say, isn't it, that the interests of the 28th Division of the BiH and DutchBat are the same?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose -- yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: In terms of defence of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were not sure that the 28th Division had the intention to defend the enclave at that stage, because they already showed that they didn't really fight on the edge of the enclave. So I don't know exactly what the objectives of the 28th Division were. They suggested that they wanted to defend the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, assuming that they had that intention, the point is this: That, as you said yourself, DutchBat's role had gone from blue to green. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- for the defence of Srebrenica, yes, that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And obviously essential to that is that DutchBat was no longer playing a neutral role.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, because we started firing on the Bosnian Serb army. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a couple of questions about the 28th Division --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- of the BiH. You said yesterday that in May you had observed them to have new uniforms; yes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But it was also the case, was it not, that in May you observed them to have some rather new shiny Kalashnikov guns, rifles.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw several new types of Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And it's also the case, isn't it, that insofar as your observations of the BiH in terms of humanitarian aid was concerned, you had some views about them hoarding the aid for their own purposes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was reported to me by the opstina itself was that the 28th Division always took a part of the supplies the UNHCR brought in for their own purpose. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But not only that, you had an opinion about that which you expressed to the parliamentary inquiry, to the Dutch government. You accept that you described that, you said that the 28th Division considered itself so important that, time and again, it reserved a large share of these stocks for the division. Do you agree --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you also made reference to what you described as the Pony Express in your evidence to the --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Just very quickly, what was the nature of the Pony Express?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Pony Express was up to 15 ponies who went out of the enclave in a southern direction, to Zepa, the enclave of Zepa, and came back with whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Cigarettes, alcohol --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For instance, later on we saw cigarettes on the market.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, just getting back to that point at which the interests of the DutchBat and the BiH are parallel at the 9th of July, prior to that time, there had been discussions, had there not, between DutchBat and the BiH about a coordinated defence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated before, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And part of that agreement was also that the weapons collection point would be emptied?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as a real attack would occur, the weapon collection point would be open to -- available for the BiH. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And your evidence yesterday, Mr. Franken, was that you described that discussion that you had with the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division as a strange discussion; yes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, is that because it was contrary to the neutral position that DutchBat was supposed to hold that you were having a discussion like that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not contrary because I had to keep up my independence, my neutrality. We had that strange discussion; yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But that's what I'm getting at is, you're right, you did have to keep up your neutrality because that was part of DutchBat mandate; you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So I couldn't coordinate a defence in the proper way. That is correct

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No, but it was a strange discussion because, in an informal sense, you were having a coordinated defence -- anticipating a coordinated defence.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were discussing the events, what would happen when an attack came, and the only coordination or, let's say, agreement, as you want to call it, is that we would stay in our OPs and defend there, and the BiH was free to defend the space between our observation posts. "OPs," I shouldn't say that. Observation posts. So there is a kind of coordination, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I've been told to slow down, Your Honour. I'm obviously just going as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if you don't ask for an extra two hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, the essence of the agreement - I call it an agreement - that you had between DutchBat and the BiH was the decision -- the agreement to withdraw, wasn't it? I'll withdraw that. Communication of the intention to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried to communicate, to coordinate both operations when an attack would occur.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And it is the case, is it not, that the BiH consistently failed to communicate their intention to withdraw to the DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know of one occasion that they tried to communicate. It was on the last period at the OP Sierra, S, way down south, and they got a fast yell from somebody, probably they should have understood that they were going, yes. But further on it never happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And, of course, that then led to the precarious situation for DutchBat in that the BiH presented itself as more of a threat than the VRS.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a conclusion I do not --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You don't agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with that. BiH was not a bigger threat than the BSA, but an uncertain factor because local commanders had their own policies.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And the result of that, what you perceived to be, renegade element in the local command resulted in the tragic death of Private van Rensen?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And not only that, there were reports, were there not, of OPs coming under fire from the BiH when DutchBat was attempting to withdraw?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not under fire, but blocked, the crews were blocked. There is one OP who - not confirmed - had fire from a direction which could not have been BSA. That was OP Mike, the situation at Mike.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: What about OP H? Wasn't there a report that OP H also came under fire from the 28th Division of the BiH?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: OP Alpha?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: OP H?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: H? No, not as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Not as you recall?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: What about OP D? Was there a report that OP D was surrounded by the 28th Division of the BiH?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: OP Delta was in the south, tried to withdraw and then was blocked and surrounded by BiH soldiers who wouldn't allow them to go in the direction of Srebrenica. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, what about when I made that statement about the threat posed by the BiH for your personnel in the observation post? There was an order issued, was there not, that members were to stay at the OPs until the arrival of the BSA, unless there was an agreement with the local BiH commander?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And is the implication -- can we infer from that, that that was as a result of the perceived threat of the BiH upon withdrawing? Is that a fair --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's as a result of the incident at OP Foxtrot, the killing of van Rensen, and didn't want to risk that the local commanders started shooting on my men.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Franken, you've given some evidence about, obviously, integral to the purpose behind the blocking positions was to prevent entry into the town of Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can the witness be shown PIC0008.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Do you have that there in front of you, Mr. Franken?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do see a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, you'll see --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Just perhaps if we go down to -- that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You'll see that there are a number of marks that have been made in the vicinity of OP U, E, and F.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, as far as you're concerned, do those markings accurately reflect the blocking positions at the south area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should divide them into -- when you see the three marks coming from uniform in the direction of what is here said, "Golf" --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that these were positions that were taken when we withdrew out of the area of Uniform and Sierra. The positions signed in in the area of Srebrenica - and there's one missing, I see - are the blocking positions that were occupied for purpose of defence of the city itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. So the three marks that we see leading up between, as you said, OP U and G, what date do you ascribe those positions as far as ...

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think these were positions taken during the 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: The 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So following on from that, insofar as the order that we saw, your original order of the 9th of July, those blocking positions are the consequence of that order?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the blocking positions directly on the south edge of the city Srebrenica, those positions in between were positions destined by the company commander withdrawing from that area. We don't drive away like hell, but then we take positions on the way down, keep a watch or an eye on our opponent.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But obviously the purpose, the strategic purpose, behind the three blocking positions that you describe as being taken on the 10th of July is that they were elevated, were they not, in terms of ...

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Elevated?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: As in there on the road --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were directly in the vicinity of the road from Zeleni Jadar to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To control that road.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And as far as the markings that have been made between OP G and H are concerned, there's a section of markings there.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: What is your evidence in respect of those markings in terms of blocking positions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three markers north of Golf, G, you have seen, are blocking positions ordered by me with the purpose to defend the city, the three red markers north of G. The other markers are positions probably designated by a company commander in order to keep contact with the Serb forces when they would come or came north.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. And can you just -- I appreciate you may not be able to be specific. Are you able to say which company commander -- is that the commander of Company B?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was Captain Groen.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, I appreciate also that while the events of the 9th and 10th of July are ongoing, you are obviously at the Potocari base --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- in the operations room.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But are you able to give any evidence as to the ability to see the town of Srebrenica itself from any of the blocking positions that have been marked on this map we have in front of us?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These blocking positions were not directed to the town itself, but they were directed on the approaches to the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The town is in a hole or in a valley, so we could probably see some of it, but the general idea is that they looked in the other direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And obviously the general idea, surely, with the blocking positions, is, once they're there, in the town, then it's too late.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, the --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: The whole point was to keep them out of the town.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of the town, yes. I could explain that, but that would be a military, technical discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: We don't need to descend into that, Mr. Franken. Now, just in relation to the blocking positions and that document that --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we can bring that up again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That original document that I showed you of the 9th of July, your seriously meant green order. Let me just take you to page 2 of that document. 2236, is it? I'm not sure whether or not you actually need to see it yourself, but your evidence was yesterday - I think we have it now - that there was an abbreviation under the heading "Coordinating Provisions," the sixth bullet point was "HRMCIS," meaning, your evidence was, be prepared for close air support, to use close air support?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And it really was the case, was it not, that the use of the blocking positions was a mechanism by which close air support could be called in?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that the purpose was to get close air support and for that purpose we arranged those blocking positions. Blocking positions -- well, I have to get technical because it's quite silly and not effective when you explore close air support, or air support anyway, to an enemy who is still moving, has free movement, in an area like that, where he has a lot of cover. We'll probably hit nothing. The general idea is, if you have a defence or whatever, an enemy is stopped by that defence, so he is more or less static; then you launch your air support, because otherwise the guys won't find them. So there is not the -- the order you give, that you want air support and that's why the blocking positions were there, is incorrect. The blocking positions were there to defend the city, and one of the means you can defend a city with is artillery and air support. The condition for air support is: Try to pin your opponent in a place or an area where the planes can find him, can see them. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Ultimately there's a relationship between the two.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Which was my point, really. -

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's all right. Is that the two were connected.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And in that regard, we looked at, yesterday, another document that you had provided -- a note that you'd provided to Captain Groen. This is a one --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I don't believe this has an evidence registration number yet, but this is the document that the English translation was provided at 12.00 yesterday. If that document could be brought up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It hasn't got a number --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the second of the two documents that were produced yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number will be 02264, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't want to delay things, but we do have hard copies of the B/C/S translations, if they haven't been received already. Okay. I understand it is in e-court. I just wanted to let everybody know that we have it, if it hasn't been received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, I just want to ask you some questions just about how this document came into existence. Now, as I understand it, your evidence was yesterday that it was a written version of a radio message from the VRS.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And it was received on or around the 10th of July. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Are you able to give any evidence as to the original source of the radio message? Who relayed this information to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously the Bosnian Serbs used one of my APCs they took from the OPs, and one of the NCOs, being a POW, read that over that radio contact. So it came in on our command net.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you heard it on the radio, you said.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it partially. I heard it on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. And when you heard it, did you create -- you made notes or wrote it down --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ops officer or the chief ops wrote it down and I took his text to inform Captain Groen.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. So these are just -- in other words, this is, perhaps, your interpretation; is it fair -- this is your interpretation of what was described as the ultimatum from the VRS. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When somebody writes something you heard, it's always an interpretation. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you also, then, obviously are responsible for what comes under the heading "UN Reaction," I presume. You wrote it as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote it as well, yes, but then the UN reaction was already known, so I didn't write this message immediately after it came in from the BSA. But I obviously waited for the UN reaction and then compiled it and sent it to Groen.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Because you appreciate that, as the document currently reads, insofar as the UN ultimatum is concerned, it's incomplete in the sense that it says "if not," and then there is nothing there. And that's certainly the case for the English version and for the Dutch version.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps if you just scroll down to the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you'll see it says: "UN reaction" --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- and then says: "If not, full column." I mean, really, the essence of the UN ultimatum there was air-strikes, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And they were described by your superior, Colonel Karremans, to the representatives of the BiH as massive air-strikes. Is that --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct, in the night of the 10th to the 11th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And that there was a warning that -- well, that obviously Mr. Karremans informed the representatives of the BiH that the southern area of the enclave would be a zone of death. I appreciate you may not have been at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not at the meeting, so I don't know what words he used. But within the procedures of air support, we know the killing zone. Killing zone is an area where you try to amass your enemy and be sure that there are none of your own troops in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So if there were evidence in this trial to the effect that they were, in fact, the words of Colonel Karremans, you would accept that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be. Could be.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'd like to take you to the 11th of July, and, again, we have established that you are at the headquarters at Potocari on that day.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But you received a request, did you not, from Captain Groen, who was the commander of B Company --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: B Company, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- which is situated in the town of Srebrenica, to divert the refugees in the direction of Potocari. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, he suggested to do so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And you granted that request.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. So you would agree with the proposition that the movement of -- the stream of refugees from B Company down to Potocari was the result of an initiative taken by Captain Groen.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially, because there has been a movement before on the initiative of the people itself. It was then stopped by the 28th Division. The situation in Srebrenica was out of control, which meant that Groen was not able to perform his orders, to defend the city, because people were in panic and crawling. And then he tried to lead them, in fact, to Potocari by putting some soldiers in front of the column and started to walk in the direction of Potocari. So, in that way, it was an initiative of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. You also gave evidence of having received reports of massive shelling --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- in the town of Srebrenica on the 10th of July, including the compound. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And so much so that you basically said to your personnel, "Well, don't bother filling in the forms anymore if there's that much shelling going on." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And despite what you described as massive shelling, you received reports of wounded only. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. That was your evidence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever, in that regard, receive any reports from the MSF, who was present in the town of Srebrenica, of the numbers of wounded in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they came to -- in the end, when they were evacuated to our compound, I heard, well, probably numbers, but I don't recollect them, how much, because it was pretty filled, yeah. But I don't know numbers. The only thing I know is that when they came in I had, what, 114 wounded brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I don't know what the total number was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No. But as for that specific -- the reports that we're talking about in terms of the shelling of the town of Srebrenica itself and what the result there was, you simply received no evidence as to the numbers.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: The reports --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had some reports about it that would mean that there were more, or something. Our attention was a bit drawn to the BSA, not to the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, turning to the next day, the 12th of July, Mr. Franken, your was that on the morning of the 12th you were being debriefed by Colonel Karremans as to his meeting, his final meeting, with General Mladic at the Hotel Fontana. And as that was going on, buses and trucks arrived. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah. And you were speaking to an officer, a G4 from Pale, who was in charge of what we called -- what one called "the evacuation of the population." Do you recall that that was your evidence yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my evidence, yes. Later on that afternoon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But you would certainly not state to this Trial Chamber that the afternoon -- the morning or the afternoon of the 12th of July was the first time you were made aware of a plan to evacuate the refugees?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No. Because, in your mind - in your mind - you were under the impression that the evacuation was something that was pre-arranged between the UN - and I'm not talking about DutchBat; I'm talking about the UN, being UNPROFOR - and General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of the evacuation first on the night before, of course. We knew that something would happen in that direction, in evacuation, because on the -- I recollect the second meeting Colonel Karremans had with Mladic, there was already talk about this event, more or less, and then I got the details when Colonel Karremans came back from the third meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. But you specifically -- you were subject to a number of debriefings, obviously, on your return from Srebrenica. You had the Assen debriefing.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back in Holland, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And in the course of your debriefing on the 7th of September, 1995, your statement was that the evacuation of the refugees was arranged and laid down on paper between General Mladic and General Smith.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Okay. Sorry, I didn't understand, obviously, which event you meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And General Smith was based in Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: He was General Nicolai's superior?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And that was your understanding of the role between each of those parties; that there was --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- an agreement and it was laid down on paper.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an agreement. The fact that it was laid down on paper I discovered when I was back in Holland. At that very moment, I didn't see that paper obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No, no. That's all right. And your other statement in that regard was the role of the battalion in this was to implement it, being DutchBat's role was to implement the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role was to make sure that it was as humanitarian as possible, et cetera, et cetera. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But those were your words. You didn't qualify -- in your statement on the 7th of September, 1995, you didn't qualify it in that regard, as you are now --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said implemented. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- you just said it was to implement it. All right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And, furthermore, DutchBat had received guidelines for this from UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you later described those guidelines as vague. You described them as vague guidelines at some stage in your evidence elsewhere. But are you able to indicate to the Trial Chamber, first of all, were the guidelines oral, or were they written?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got them oral by Colonel Karremans; later on I saw them written.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. You got them orally from Colonel Karremans on the 12th of July - is that correct - or the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12th.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: After he came back from his meeting with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came back and he had contact with the UN again. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Sorry, you mean he came -- Colonel Karremans had contact with the UN again, meaning phone contact?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I say, he used the phone.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Do you know in particular who he was in contact with?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: It could have been General Nicolai; it could have been General Brantz --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he doesn't know, Ms. Condon, he doesn't know. I mean, it could be whoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You indicated that you saw them -- later on, you saw the guidelines in written form.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I got something on paper. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And can you indicate when you received those guidelines?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really. I suppose it was on the 12th, because there was a lot of messaging and ordering coming up and down the line, in the UN line. So I suppose it was on the 12th, but I was a bit busy in those days.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'm not criticising you for the fact that you can't remember.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, are you able to indicate specifically where the guidelines came from?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only can presume where they came from. Logically, it would have been Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, no presumptions --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- I mean, we only require informed answers from you, not presumptions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the witness be shown 1D00035, please, at page -- and I'd like -- perhaps I'll just identify the document, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Do you have that in front of you, Mr. Franken?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You see the cover page of this document is a communication between Mr. Akashi from Zagreb. You obviously know who he was.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know who he was. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A special delegation, special functionary for the UN, for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And there are a number of people, obviously, who this document is being distributed to, one of whom we can see appears to be General Smith, at Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And ultimately it's to Mr. Annan, who was the then Under-Secretary.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And we should, perhaps, identify that it's dated the 12th of July, 1995, and it appears, although it is quite faint, that the time at which -- there is a time stamp of 1322 on this document, in the upper right-hand corner. You may or may not be able to see that on the version that you have. Let's take you to page 2 of the document, at paragraph 5, and you just see -- perhaps if you read that paragraph to the point where we see it says, "The plans of UNHCR and UNPF, conveyed yesterday in my Z-1139 to evacuate all those people from Srebrenica wishing to leave, have encountered at least initial resistance from Bosnian government authorities." And then I just draw your attention to the third sentence in this paragraph, which reads: "However, at a meeting at 7.45 local time today, with the UNHCR Sarajevo representative and the UNPROFOR Civil Affairs Coordinator, Bosnian Minister Muratovic made the following points: "(a) local Bosnian officials in Srebrenica are not authorised to negotiate on behalf of the Bosnian government, at least until proper communications can be established with them." Now, just in that regard, in terms of Mr. Muratovic, it was the case, was it not, that one of the members of what became known as the refugee committee, Mr. Mandic, with your assistance --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- and your persistence, no doubt, managed to actually make contact on the 12th of July with Mr. Muratovic's office.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just with his office or some aide de guerre or something. But he didn't make contact with Mr. Muratovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No, I'm not suggesting that he made contact. But your perception, because the contact, obviously, never eventuated, but your perception of that was that Mr. Mandic was brushed aside with a story that Mr. Muratovic was at dinner and he didn't want to be disturbed. That's how you saw it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. But that was your opinion that you expressed to the NIOD report, as it --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not only my opinion. When Mandic told me what was going on, I got a bit angry and took the phone myself --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Of course you did --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and then I heard the same story again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You were brushed aside yourself.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. Now, there are a number of other conditions that are outlined in this document here insofar as the question of evacuation is concerned. And then, paragraph 6, you'll see that there is a statement to the effect that -- if I can focus your mind on the third sentence: "The BSA also said that they would arrange and provide the transportation for the departure of the population from Srebrenica to Tuzla." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. Now, is it fair to say that this document insofar as it reflects that it was an UNPROFOR plan to evacuate the refugees from Srebrenica, that this document is a reflection of how you understood the situation to be? Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that very moment, it's not fair to say so. The only thing I had was that the UN told me how to act on behalf of the evacuation. And I didn't read this before, so I can't say whether the complete text of that document covers that, what my mind was at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but you obviously didn't have the benefit of the specifics, as outlined in this document.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But insofar as the essence of the document is concerned and what your perception was, which you've just told us about, that it was agreed between Smith and Mladic --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- you would agree that this document reflects that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It confirms my idea at that moment that the UN had at least consented in the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And you found yourself in the rather strange position, did you not, of the same people that had ordered you to defend Srebrenica and obviously launch an offensive insofar as the VRS was concerned, within 24 hours, you've been ordered to assist.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, in fact, within three hours, because the very morning, on the 12th, I got another order to defend.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: On the morning of the 12th, so it was even closer.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've got to be flexible.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But the issue then arose, did it not, that the UN, UNPROFOR, didn't appreciate, the higher-ups, being General Nicolai and Gobillard didn't appreciate the logistical problems that DutchBat had?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When you say that -- well --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The logistical problems were reported to Nicolai. I know that General Nicolai said that the battalions should do it themselves, if you're referring to that, and I made it quite clear that it was absolutely impossible. But further on, I don't know whether the logistical problems of the battalion played any role in their decision to consent in the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But, as you've -- you've described it like this in the past, in terms of your evidence to the parliamentary inquiry. What you said was: "Mladic made an offer to the UN to do it themselves, but the UN said they were not able to and then approved Mladic doing it, because that is what happened."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I understand happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So the issue there was that DutchBat had some difficulties, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite a lot then. Which ones are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, in terms of -- I'm not referring to the question of fuel, but just in relation to the physical, logistical means of carrying out the transport efficiently.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And we've already heard evidence that you had food that would last for only 40 hours from the 11th of July; yes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something like that --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You've got terrible --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- But just for the strength of my battalion, not for 30.000 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. You've got extreme temperatures in terms of the heat in July out there.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you would agree, would you not, that this evacuation was necessary for the welfare of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. And if it had to be done, it had to be done quickly.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to move to another topic. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break, starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, if the witness could be shown 1D36.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That document should actually be in front of you, Mr. Franken. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps if we have a closer look at this document. This an UNMO situation report that you, no doubt, will be familiar with. Not this report specifically but reports of this nature.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And if we could turn, please, to page 4 of this report. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You'll see at the top, headed, "Srebrenica Update 12046B," the code there is the 12th of July, at 0746 hours. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Local time. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And if I can just draw your attention to paragraph 5 of that document, you'll see there that there is a statement to the effect, "The DutchBat DCO ..." That's you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: "... says that in case of evacuation, UNPROFOR would provide about 20 buses and make more trips." Now, is that correct, that you did make that statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that statement. No, absolutely not. I don't know, I never saw this document before, but as far as I am concerned, that's a different DCO.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: There's one and only --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's only one, sorry, but I didn't make that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. So you would say that insofar as this report, this UNMO report reflects that, it's simply inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: What is your evidence to the Trial Chamber about, generally, the accuracy of these UNMO reports?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm familiar with these kinds of reports but we never got them. It was not -- in the reporting system, DutchBat didn't get the UNMO reports. Once in a while I saw them, but it was not in the normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Do you agree with this proposition: That often the UNMOs would rely upon DutchBat -- that they would get their information from DutchBat to compile these reports?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't know, because I never saw the report so I can't confirm or deny that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Well, insofar as, obviously, the next statement is -- well, before I go to that, you would say, wouldn't you, that that statement as to the provision of 20 buses doesn't reflect the fact that DutchBat had no fuel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does not reflect -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. I'll rephrase that. Is it if UNPROFOR were -- if DutchBat were to provide buses for the evacuation, just in theory, implicit in that would also be that they had fuel, obviously for transport.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, and we did not have it. But we didn't have 20 buses as well, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. I also return to the debriefing that you received from Colonel Karremans when he returned from his final meeting with General Mladic. Now, your evidence has been that you didn't really get an opportunity to get much detail from Colonel Karremans, because, as that was going on, suddenly buses and trucks were arriving. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But what you have said -- perhaps I'll just -- I'll show you your statement of the 26th and 27th of September, just so that there is no dispute. This is 1D33. Now, that's the front page of your statement. Do you see that in front of you, Mr. Franken?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's familiar, that statement that you made for this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: If we go to page 5 of this statement, I just want to -- and there is a -- yes, that's it. Paragraph -- if we can just make it a little larger, if possible, a bit further -- if we scroll down, please, Madam Usher. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That paragraph beginning, "Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans was away for two and a half hours," so just to focus your mind on the time here, it is most definitely the morning of the 12th of July, 1995; yes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And what you do say is that he briefed you quickly, but "he was able to tell me that Mladic told him how he wanted the evacuation to be carried out."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. "Separation of the men from the rest was discussed, as well as when DutchBat was to evacuate." And then, in particular, there are particular details provided to you by Colonel Karremans as to how Mladic wanted the evacuation carried out. Do you see that there? In batches? "Mladic said who should be evacuated first: The wounded" --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: "-- women, children and DutchBat." And then you say, "Karremans did not agree with this." That's what you say in the statement.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it says so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'm not criticising you, Mr. Franken. I'm just -- and obviously the basis for that is Franken -- Colonel Franken [sic] saying to you, he proposed these evacuations in batches and I disagreed with it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
