utterances.text: Well, what he said to me, obviously, was that he didn't agree with the way Mladic wanted it to be executed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: In that specific, as we see, five -- the provision of five batches, if you like, is the way it's described.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I see it here. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to show you 1D24, and I want to take you to page 4 of that document. Now, you'll just see from the cover page, this is the NIOD report which, no doubt, you are familiar with and, in fact, you were interviewed for.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was interviewed. And I'm not familiar with the complete report.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'm sure you've got better things to do in your spare time. But if you could just go to page 4, and there is a particular paragraph, the final paragraph, if we just scroll down, that begins: "In order to get clarification ..." Do you see that there, "In order to get clarification ..."?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. I'll read it out. "In order to get clarification as to how this was all going to be done, Boering and Rave were sent back to Bratunac, while Karremans went to report to Colonel Brantz." Now, I don't think we've established, but Colonel Brantz was who?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was staff of the HQ -- UNPROFOR HQ in Tuzla, sector north-east, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: "Apart from the question of the surrender and disarming of the ABiH and some comment on the improved atmosphere of the negotiations, the most important bit of information that Karremans had for Brantz was the plan to organise the evacuation in five batches." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: "The first one would be the seriously wounded and wounded, the next batch would be the weak, followed by the stronger women and children, then men aged 17 to 60, and lastly DutchBat itself." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you also see that: "The situation report in which Brantz passed on this plan for an evacuation in batches showed that he expected that afternoon to see a start being made only on the evacuation of the first batch - the wounded and the seriously wounded." Do you see it there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there was an added remark in relation to batch four being -- "will be subject to debriefing by the VRS." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So you agree it appears from that communication that Colonel Karremans had for Colonel Brantz, that, in fact, Colonel Karremans was proposing that the evacuation be conducted in five batches.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or Colonel Karremans informed Colonel Brantz what the plan of Mladic was. I really don't know. I see this for first time in my life. And it was not part of the communication between Brantz and Karremans, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, just in relation to that final notation there, "will be subjected to debriefing by the VRS," you see that there --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- about the men?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: There was a perception, was there not, that there were hardly any able-bodied men in and around the compound at Potocari, held by DutchBat. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fair is that we saw not many men. That's correct, yes, in that stage, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Well, we'll return to that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay? Insofar as the provision of fuel was concerned, your statement and your evidence has been that there was no question in your mind that there was an agreement in relation to the provision of fuel by UNPROFOR for the evacuation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the end I was ordered to give fuel to the BSA; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. But just before we get to that point where you were ordered to provide fuel after the evacuation --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- in your -- on your 13th of September, 1995, debriefing, what you said was that "the agreements on the evacuation of the refugees stated that UNPROFOR would supply the fuel."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: "Whether Smith or Karremans made this arrangement, he did not know."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So, obviously, in your mind, you had received information at some stage that it was either one of them.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously somebody in the UN decided that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: "Because there was a fuel shortage in the battalion, Mladic supplied it himself initially, and there was talk of an arrangement in exchange for its use afterwards."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now I put this proposition to you: Was it the case that there was some fuel available to DutchBat to proceed with the evacuation? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be short, the fuel situation was quite clear. In all my vehicles, I had one -- they have two tanks of fuel; one was filled or partially filled. And I had about 2.000, 3.000 litres in my tanks, my supply tanks. That's all. So that wouldn't be hardly enough to make one shift.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. As far as you're aware, was any of the 2.000 or 3.000 that was in your reserve used at all for the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No? None at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. So your evidence is that what happened was that, in effect, there was -- the VRS advanced the fuel to UNPROFOR. Is that a fair way to describe it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, that happened, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: They said, "We'll provide you with the fuel but you have to pay us back."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't know what the arrangements were between the VRS and the UN or UNPROFOR on that level. The only thing I know is that I didn't have the fuel. They were driving cars around, so they had the fuel. And when it was ended, the evacuation, I got orders that as soon as we got fuel, to provide the BSA with the amount of fuel that was applicable for, et cetera, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And that was 27.000 litres, or something of that --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something of that amount. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And that order, you've described that order in the past as having come from Sarajevo --?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- but that obviously it would not be directly from Sarajevo because it could come through Colonel Karremans to you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, insofar as the evidence of separation is concerned and your observation, it is clear from your evidence that you, yourself, saw no separations of the men.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the actual separation. I, once in a while, saw columns of men going in the direction of the "White House." That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, your evidence has been in the past in your debriefing reports that, in fact, you saw all 239 men that were on your list, which we'll get to, board the buses with their families.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the last convoys, and in these last convoys concerning the refugees on our compound, there were 251 pulled-out men. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And also you've given evidence this morning about that document that you signed, of the 17th of July, and I appreciate that you amended it to the extent that you thought it reflected the reality of the situation, by saying insofar as DutchBat escorted the convoys, they were carried out in accordance with --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- proper conventions. However, you agree that you made no attempt, or you didn't -- it didn't occur to you in the amendment of that document to raise any issues or irregularities about the process of the evacuation generally. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Again, I'm not criticising you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And obviously -- the obvious irregularities lie in the reports of the nine dead bodies and the one fellow who one of your personnel said he'd seen executed.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. I know you've been asked about this before. Your response in relation to the nine dead, initially, when Mr. Nuhanovic came to you, didn't he, and said he'd overheard some UNMOs talking about nine dead bodies behind a house, you gave an unusual response, didn't you, given the seriousness of that report.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me it was probably not unusual. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, you said, "Don't spread that bullshit around."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. That's correct. It's not unusual when you have 30.000 people, half in panic, and then spreading around the story that there were nine men executed. So it's not that unusual, in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Even in that context, though, Mr. Franken, it indicates that you didn't seek to investigate it and take it seriously then.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took it seriously, seriously enough to prevent panic between the refugees, because that was the reason that I said, "Don't spread this bullshit around."

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: What about -- again, there were complaints -- all right. Well, just in relation to that issue of the report of the nine bodies, did you send one of your personnel to go -- because you've -- we have seen on the map that you marked yesterday, you were given specific information as to where those bodies were supposedly found. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was reported that it was about 60, 70 metres from the "White House," in a certain direction by the water, so my conclusion was that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. But, naturally, having taken that report seriously, you would then send one of your personnel down to investigate.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why? When an officer reporting to me, a good officer, he told me what happened, exactly what happened. So why did I have to send somebody down? I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. All right. There were reports, were there not, given to you by other members of the refugee committee as to, you know, bodies being found, which you then did get people to go and investigate those locations, and nothing was found, was it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's right. So you were in a situation where it was often very difficult to distinguish between rumour and fact.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So insofar as the complaint -- the report of the one fellow who'd been executed, and that was perhaps a little bit more specific insofar as you had Captain Groenewegen telling you that he had seen from a distance soldiers, various soldiers, executing a man?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the report from Groenewegen came through the commander of Charlie Company, C Company, who was in this area, to the colonel, and the colonel told me what happened. So I didn't interfere further on in that thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: But you did give -- as I understand it, you gave -- did you not give Colonel Groenewegen some advice about putting the incident in writing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave the advice to -- not personally, but I gave the advice to put the report in writing. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, because what you'd indicated in your debriefing report of the -- I think it's the 20th of September: "It seemed important to Franken to have the witness make a note of the event in writing," which stands to reason, why that's important.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because memories of people --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: No, no. I'm -- that's very important.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, did you ever see that report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not he ever made the report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose when I give a soldier an order, as commander, that it is done. But I didn't check whether they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right. Now, finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for the record, page 52, line 4, Groen should be reading as Groenewegen.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Franken, I want to turn to the issue of the list of men that was made on your initiative. Now, we just established a moment ago that, initially, Colonel Karremans and yourself shared the perception that there was just a handful of able-bodied men in the compound.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that between the 11th and the 13th of July Colonel Karremans is very much, an understatement would be, a very busy man; yes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And he is confined, so to speak, to the headquarters, to -- he's not out and about amongst the --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you said yesterday that you made -- which is certainly to your credit, you made an effort to get out amongst -- you're around, to see what was going on, to see what was going on in and around the compound. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only an effort. I did that at least twice a day. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: So it would stand to reason, would it not, that you -- that Colonel Karremans would be heavily reliant on you - you're his deputy - for, specifically, any information as to the question of numbers of able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes? And if, in particular --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I'll take the witness -- if Mr. Franken could be shown 1D37.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a document in front of me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Again, this is a chapter from the NIOD report, and if I can just take you to page 5 of that document, and the third -- there's a paragraph that begins, "However, based on these statements..." and that's what I want to focus your mind on. But then I want to take you to the sentence that begins on the fifth line, that --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Just there is fine, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: "Karremans himself confirms..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: "Karremans himself confirms that it is true that at some point he did find out about the list but that the importance of the matter had fully escaped him at the time. There were 50.000 people crowded together in one place. I didn't even though that there were another 280 to 300 men on the compound. Franken told me about this later." Now, would that be accurate, that you would have been the source of any information to Colonel Karremans about the numbers of able-bodied men in and around the compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I don't know whether I'm the only source, but obviously I told him about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And, obviously, the list was a significant indicator, in your mind, as to what the numbers were.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: With --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: On the compound. Well, what I am -- is it -- given what you've said about the perception that there were only a handful of -- well, perhaps I'll withdraw that. I'll take you to further down in this document where it says, in the -- the next paragraph, there's a statement -- there's a sentence that begins, "From these statements..." Do you that there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: "From these statements it was already decided what Karremans had said about the small presence of men military age outside the compound."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: "Only a handful" Right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a big hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, he's talking about men outside the compound here.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Not inside.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right? What do you say about that perception held by Colonel Karremans insofar as there being a handful of or a small presence of men of military age outside the compound? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, relatively seen to the total amount of refugees, it is a small amount, of course, because there were about, in my estimation, 600 or 700 and there were about 25.000, 30.000 people outside there. So, relatively seen, it's a small amount. But I can't read Colonel Karremans' mind, why he said "a handful."

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I appreciate you can't read his mind. But you would, obviously, disagree strenuously with the proposition that the number of 251 to 300 as being a total number of men of able -- able-bodied men in and around the compound, you would disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's incorrect. The number 251 was the -- about 60, 70, didn't want to be registered, so about 300 were in the compound and the estimation was that there were about 600 outside the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you now back to 1D36, at page 4. This is that UNMO situation report. And at page 4 of the situation report --

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, 1D36. No, no, that's not the right. 1D36 is the UNMO situation report. We've seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: It's the one that you didn't agree with the paragraph that was reflecting your statements. This is it. Page 4 of that document, and paragraph 6, at page 4. You see there it says: "CO DutchBat ..." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: "CO DutchBat was told by BSA that they have been given an ultimatum for the BiH soldiers in the compound to hand over all their weapons by 1000 hours today."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And "today" is probably the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It then goes on to say: "There are no armed BiH soldiers in the compound." However, you would agree, would you not, that it was extremely difficult, if not impossible, to distinguish between a civilian and a BiH soldier when it came to able-bodied men?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Because uniforms were an indication.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and parts of uniforms could be an indication as well, but that didn't prove anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And in that regard, after the refugees left, in and around the compound there were weapons found, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two small arms found in the latrines; yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, your description in your debriefing report was just "weapons." You weren't specific.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And furthermore, insofar as the baggage that was left lying around the "White House" was burned, which we heard about yesterday, a consider number of small arms ammunition exploded. That was your report to the debriefing.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Just pardon me a moment, Your Honour. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Congratulations. Thank you, Ms. Condon. I couldn't understand exactly who was going next. I know who is going third, but I didn't -- Mr. Stojanovic? Mr. Stojanovic will be cross-examining you; he appears for accused Borovcanin here, together with Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Stojanovic, he is all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Franken. Before this testimony, you appeared on the 15th of September, in 2003, in the Blagojevic case as a witness. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recollect, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, you testified that shortly before the operation by the Army of Republika Srpska in Srebrenica, there were several attacks from the Srebrenica enclave towards the territory under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recollect two attacks reported. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us a little more about these two attacks that you talked about.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As was reported to me by, as I recollect, OP Mike -- sorry, M, observation post M, there were burning houses in the north of the enclave. There was some small-calibre fire heard overnight. That is one. Later on, in a contact with Major Nikolic of the Bratunac Brigade, he indicated that it had been an attack of BiH forces over there. And the second one was an ambush in the area south of the enclave, Zeleni Jadar, you could say, on the way to Zepa, where the BSA told us that seven or nine soldiers were killed in an ambush led by -- obviously, by the BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just so that I can understand, whose soldiers were killed at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnian Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when this happened? Which month in 1995, based on your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, but I'm try to go think of it. It must be around May, I suppose. Yes. April/May, as far as I recollect, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that the burning of the village was on the 26th of June, 1995? Is this date possible?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it part of your mandate in the Srebrenica enclave to prevent this incident and similar incidents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you believe, in view of the objective position that you were in, that you successfully carried out your mandate in terms of this particular point?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your correctness. Please allow me to show you a part of the text that you wrote entitled "In the Name of Peace - Retrospective."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the purposes of identification, this is Exhibit 2D41. I would like the usher to place the English version on the ELMO so that we can all follow the text, because this document is still not in the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, can you please tell us when you drafted this text.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should be somewhere in 1996, I suppose. Early 1996 or late 1995. I don't know exactly. That book was published, as I recollect, in 1996, so somewhere shortly before that I wrote that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, you state: "And then the bomb arrived, an order arrived, of course, an oral order to assist the Serbs --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that we are not looking at the original of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "-- which were given the approval to evacuate the population with their own vehicles." Do you see that, Mr. Franken?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not see that, but I heard the text and I recognised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I heard the interpreters point out that they could not follow because they were not seeing it on the screen. Madam Usher, what's the problem, as such? It is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3, paragraph 2 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's there so that the witness can have a good look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see it now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The last six lines, basically, of that paragraph that you see on the screen now. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is, Mr. Franken: When you were writing this and when you said that the Serbs had permission to proceed with the deportation of the population with their own vehicles, can you actually tell us who issued or who had granted this permission?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do not know. The UN did, and who in the UN, I do not know, because Colonel Karremans always had the contacts to the higher echelons, so I can't name a general or a person. But it came down the UN line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So is my conclusion correct when I say that, based on your understanding, it's not in dispute that the Serbs were given permission to evacuate the population with their own vehicles; but now, today, you cannot say exactly who from the UN system granted this permission. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would -- since you've already responded to a series of questions by my learned friend, I would like to put the following question to you: Did, if I understand correctly, and I'm speaking of the Dutch Battalion, they at one point give the Army of Republika Srpska about 27.000 litres of fuel for the requirements of this evacuation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was afterwards, but it did happen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us approximately when this occurred.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, somewhere around the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that point, the evacuation had already been completed as far as the civilian population was concerned. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And as you said today, it was your mandate to act for the purposes of the evacuation on the 12th and the 13th of July in accordance with the permission that had been granted?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And that is what you did; that is how you conducted yourself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as we were allowed to, yes, I did, or we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, 1995, the civilian population was in front of the headquarters of the B Company and set off from there, from Srebrenica, towards the UN base in Potocari. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at one point members of the 28th Division stopped the column of refugees on the road and asked them to return to the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's also another occasion. That happened on the night or evening of the 10th. And the movement on the 11th, led in by personnel of B Company, then there was no 28th Division anymore so nobody stopped that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the reason that the 28th Division of the BiH army would not allow the civilian population to go from Srebrenica to Potocari, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not know. I was a bit puzzled about it, but I did not know. I only can guess, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your information, how long were the members of the 28th Division in Srebrenica, until what time? And when were they on the Srebrenica-Potocari road?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the road Srebrenica-Potocari there were the civilians, refugees. The last sign we had of the 28th Division was in the late evening of the 10th when the colonel saw quite a lot of armed men on the marketplace, in the city itself. Afterwards, we never heard or saw anything about that 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For purposes of clarification, when you say "colonel," does that mean that you are thinking of Colonel Karremans? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I say "colonel," I mean Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans, CO of DutchBat. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I am going to ask you to look at an excerpt of video footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is V006822, and the 65 ter number is P02016. We are going to look at the segment from 9.40 to 9.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, do you recognise the weapon that is slung across the shoulder of the member of the Dutch Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's an FAL 7.62 infantry gun, or infantry rifle, I should say. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who is the manufacturer of this rifle? Can you please help us?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: FN Browning, Belgium.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at another segment, which is marked V0003914. The 65 ter number is P2007. And it's a segment from 55.28 to 56.10.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, this is a segment -- before we actually look at it, this is material taken on the 16th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we freeze here for a second. We don't have to look at the whole segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So this is footage taken on the 16th of July, 1995, when members of the 28th Division of the BiH army crossed into the territory of the village of Nezuk, which was under the control of the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you see this rifle slung across the back of the BiH army member?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this rifle was from the same batch of weapons that we just saw, which was something the member of the Dutch Battalion was carrying?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same type of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that this weapon was taken from members of the Dutch Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible, but I don't know what date this picture is exactly. I know that the crew of Charlie Company had been attacked or -- attacked, no, overwhelmed by about 30, 40 Muslims, and they took then their weapons, et cetera, so ... "Observation Post Charlie," I meant, C. It's in the south-west of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did members of your unit at OP Charlie have weapons like this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at another short segment, which is three minutes long, and it's marked V0003676. The 65 ter number is P02017.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And before we see the footage, I just want to say this is a section that depicts the members of the 28th Division coming into the territory of the village of Nezuk on the 16th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We are looking at this footage, Mr. Franken, and I would like you just to focus on the weapons that are carried by the people in this segment, and then I will have some questions about the weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop, stop, stop, stop. Since you intervened to tell the witness what he should be paying careful attention to, do you want to start the footage again? Because I think we were not paying particular attention to that, in any case. So let's start the footage running again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, do you agree that practically all the members of this column are men with weapons, armed men?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I saw, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: They have different kinds of infantry weapons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: By the way, I would like to ask you if you recognise the person now in front of you in this particular frame.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to try to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ID number 4D26. It's a Defence exhibit, ERN number 01827752, 7752. It's an order by the B&H army commander Rasim Delic of the 6th of August, 1995. Could the usher please assist because the document has now been translated and the translation is in the system as of today. But I'm not sure whether we can use it now. Maybe we can just place it on the ELMO and then focus on the bottom of the first page and the top of the second page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, this is an order by the BiH army commander, Rasim Delic, and as you can see on page 1 of this document, this order is dated 6th August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And it was sent to the command of the 2nd Corps of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to draw your attention to one paragraph under 2. The title is "Mobilisation Preparations" or "Organisational Preparations." It says here that: "The newly formed 9th Liberation Brigade will be replenished from the ranks of volunteers, and the following units will become part of the 9th Liberation Brigade as their organisational parts." And I'm drawing your attention to the second page in which it says that: "Amongst others, on the strength of the 9th Muslim Liberation Brigade, a unit called Mudzahid is to find its place and it is now on the strength of the 28th Division and it has 94 troops." My question to you is this: Are you aware of the fact that, under the 283rd Brigade of the 28th Division of BiH army, a company had been formed earlier on and the name of that company was Mudzahid?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that. I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, I will not insist on this document. I would kindly ask you to assist us with the following subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank the usher. We will no longer need this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Observation Post Papa was in the north of the enclave, in the vicinity of the Yellow Bridge. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, 1995, in the morning hours, from that direction, the troops of the VRS started moving towards Potocari. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Once the members of the Dutch Battalion hoisted a white flag, these troops skirted the check-point and continued moving towards Potocari. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Help us, please, and tell us: How long did the members of the Dutch Battalion stay in the Papa observation point near the Yellow Bridge?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just thinking. Papa was withdrawn on the 13th or the 14th. I don't know exactly. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And this withdrawal from the Papa observation point, did it follow your order, or did they do that of their own will?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A withdrawal is always done on order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any of the members who had manned the Papa point get captured or did they all return to the base?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recollect, Papa returned completely to the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you spoke about the information that you had received about the killing of nine persons and one civilian as two completely separate events, and this was on page 78, 79, and 81 of yesterday's testimony provided by Mr. Franken. Do you remember that you told us about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who provided you with this information? Actually, the two separate pieces of information.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the killing of the nine persons was reported to me by First Lieutenant Coster; and the information of the execution of the single person came to me through Colonel Karremans and was reported by the soldier who saw it, through the company commander, C Company, towards the colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever told who the dead bodies were, who the persons were who had been killed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you never learned the identity of the persons who had shot at those men.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You also never learned when the persons had been executed, as it was claimed that they were.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the nine men are concerned, we did not know the exact timing. The report of the soldier was the actual execution, so the timing of that execution, we knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to this soldier's report, when did the execution take place, the execution of the nine persons?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sorry, I have to correct you. The soldier reported the single execution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think he testified on this in the most clear manner yesterday. I don't think we need to go through it again. He made the distinction between one case and the other, who gave the information, and that's when Mr. Bourgon intervened as well. So any further questions which were not on matters that were not covered yesterday, yes, by all means, because this is related to one of the charges; but otherwise, please, let's avoid repetitions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion you also mentioned a facility that you referred to as the "White House." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't hear the interpreter. I'm just reading the text now. Hold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The counsel is referring you to that part of the testimony where you referred to the "White House."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose he will be following up with a few questions. Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, how long did you refer to that house as the "White House" in your vocabulary?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the moment that it was occupied or used by the BSA, it was called the "White House" and ever stayed so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, on pages 71 and 72 of the transcript, you said that records were kept of the number of men who entered the "White House," and that the same number of men left the "White House." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that concerns the period that the UNMOs were there. They kept a number of the men entering and going out, and in time that was the beginning of the afternoon of the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The record on the number of men who entered and left the house, was it kept on the 13th of July as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As soon as the UNMOs had to withdraw, we didn't keep up numbering.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that you don't know whether, on the 13th of July, there were any men in the "White House" who might have left the "White House" as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that does not mean. We knew that all the time there were men in the "White House" and afterwards transported with that light blue bus. The only thing I do not know is the exact number of men.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the night between the 12th and the 13th of July, you stayed at the UN base. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During that night and in the morning of the 13th, did you receive any information about any killings that had occurred during that night?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I think that was the night that it got reported, the suicides that we mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we heard that yesterday. Allow me to draw your attention to the part of your testimony in the Blagojevic case that is relative to the role of Momir Nikolic. During that testimony, on page 1557 of the transcript dated 15 September, you said, amongst other things, that, on the 15th of July, Momir Nikolic had arrived in the UN base, by car, and you also said that those car belonged to your mechanics. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I presume Momir Nikolic is Major Nikolic from the Bratunac Brigade, then I remember that. That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you help us, please. How come that Major Nikolic found himself in the possession of the car that belonged to your mechanic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You'd better ask Major Nikolic. I do not know. I just saw this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We will ask him, but I wanted to hear from you first whether you have any knowledge, because you mentioned it. Let me put it to you in another way. Do you know at any point in time Major Nikolic requisitioned that vehicle from your mechanic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know at any point in time. I only can repeat what I said before in other testimony. There was a rumour that the mechanic had made a deal with Major Nikolic, point, and then I saw Major Nikolic coming in with his car.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And this mechanic of yours, was he a Dutch person or a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was a -- he was a local, a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Why did he arrive on the 15th of July? What did he want from you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Nikolic came in -- yes, sorry. He wanted me to pay the bill of the hotel where the POWs were held, and asked for the rent of the location the UNMOs obviously had in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the rent of the location," do you mean -- do you mean that he asked for money for the rent of those locations, for the use of those locations?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He, or the owner of the hotel, asked for money for the food he obviously gave to the POWs, and Major Nikolic asked for the rent of a bureau, or whatever, in Bratunac. Obviously, the UNMOs did that or rented that or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you give him the money?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was your impression of the position that Momir Nikolic held in those days?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Asked for -- every time he gave another job he had at the Bratunac Brigade that differed from the CO and operations officer, he said he was, anyway, a major of the Bratunac Brigade, and we always considered him as the actual liaison to the Bosnian Serb army, because the official one, Colonel Vukovic, was seldom reachable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday and today you spoke about the compiling of the list of able-bodied men in the UN base. Did Nesib Mandzic participate in the compiling of that list?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that his name was not on the list?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not notice. I -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then there's no point in me asking you why his name is not there, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And finally let me ask you this: What about Ramiz Becirovic? You mentioned his name yesterday on direct. Did you personally have any contacts with Ramiz Becirovic, before the 11th of July, that is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Ramiz Becirovic, being the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division, I suppose, is the man -- when I spoke to the 28th Division, he was always my counterpart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We've heard testimony by a member of the DutchBat who said that Ramiz Becirovic asked you to provide him with asylum, protection in the UN base. Did he address you personally with such request?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what about his wife? Did she come to you at any point in time to ask for protection from you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not -- none of them came personally to me for protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that his wife was at the UN base between the 12th and the 13th of July, 1995, together with other refugees?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, could be, but there were 30.000 of them, so -- and I didn't know them all personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, I'm going to show you Ramiz Becirovic's statement. The number is 4D2 and the ERN number is 01854518 to 4532. Since this statement is in the e-court, I would like to draw your attention to the last paragraph on page 7 and the first paragraph of page 8 of this statement. This is where Ramiz Becirovic says this: Before the aggression against Srebrenica, he had some 140.000 -- for all of us to be able to follow, the English version is page 9, paragraph 3. Page 9, paragraph 3. He says that he's had about 140.000 of the then-German marks and that this money was left with his wife. And when she arrived in Tuzla, he asked her what happened to the money, and then she informed him that, in Potocari, when the Chetniks did the search, she had buried that money in the sand that was in the barrel in the akumulator factory where it was. And this was within the UNPROFOR compound, according to him. Mr. Franken, do you know anything about this money at all? Were there any comments to the effect that that money was later on found or taken away from anybody?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, what's the relevance of this? Starting from Madam Becirovic's presence in the compound and now Mr. Becirovic's statement about money in Srebrenica, what's the relevance of this, especially in relation to your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the indictment, my client is charged with the confiscation of money and valuables from the refugees who were in Potocari. Since my -- to my last question, Mr. Franken said that he never saw Mrs. Becirovic. I will withdraw this question, but I believe that my point, however, was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution did not adduce any evidence as yet in relation to possible confiscation or possession of this particular amount of money. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We didn't have it in the records, so we've heard nothing about it until you put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have it in the indictment, Your Honour, and since the Prosecution gave up on Mr. Karremans' testimony, it seemed to me that this was my last chance to put a question of this sort. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, I would like to ask you this: Do you know anything about the requisition of money or seizing of money from the refugees who were on the UN base on the 12th and the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As long as they were on the UN base, there was no requisition of anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, and this completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank the honourable Chamber for the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. I think we thank you, too. We are having a break in four minutes' time, so we might as well have it now, Mr. Bourgon, and you will start your cross -- if you are in agreement, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have a 25-minute break, starting now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Bourgon is appearing for Mr. Nikolic in this case, and he will be cross-examining you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As was indicated to you by the President of the Trial Chamber, I represent Drago Nikolic in this case. Now, during your testimony yesterday, you referred to four officers of the Bosnian Serb army with whom you had some dealings during the relevant period, and I would just like to confirm that these four officers are Vukotic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Colonel Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Acemovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Major Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Bratunac Brigade, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Regarding Acemovic and Jankovic, those were, according to you, two colonels reporting to General Mladic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said they came from Pale. They never told me that they would report to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's fine with me. I can live with this answer, for sure. As for Vukotic, you mentioned in your testimony yesterday -- sorry, in your testimony in the Krstic case, that he was from the Skelani Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as we knew, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as far as Major Nikolic goes, you mentioned yesterday that he was from Bratunac Brigade and that he was the liaison to the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our liaison to the Bosnian Serb army. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you also said something that I would like to confirm, where you said that you had to deal with a couple of brigades during the relevant time, and you mention Skelani Brigade, Bratunac Brigade, and you also said - and I quote from page 14, lines 16 to 18 - that you had contact in the Milici area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what we called the Milici Brigade. But "contact" you'll have to give that the context of visual contact, not actually. The only point we actually had contact with are the both mentioned, Major Nikolic and Colonel Vukotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As a follow-up to your answer, there's one thing I would like to confirm with you and that is, in relation to these events, and that is, of course, from 16 July to 17 July, that you did not encounter anyone from the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, given that you, at some point in time, acted as the S2 for DutchBat - S2, for some people who might not know what that means, the intelligence officer - in some respect, towards the end, you're nevertheless familiar with the existence of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We knew that there was a military unit over there. We never referred to it as the Zvornik Brigade, but we knew there was a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, to your knowledge, the Zvornik Brigade was not involved in these events, the relevant events, in July of 1995, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We couldn't identify any Bosnian Serb units, sir, so, to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, going back to Major Nikolic from the Bratunac Brigade. A question was put to you by my colleague, and you said that many times he would give you different positions.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that, in the end, it was not possible for you to determine what exactly his position was.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Our idea or our conclusion was that he had some job on brigade level, but that's it, not what job.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in a statement that you gave to the OTP, and that was a statement that you gave on the 26th and 27th of September, 1995, to the Prosecutor, do you remember the approximate time-frame of giving that statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I gave a lot of statements in the last 11 years, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, I don't think -- if there's a need, I can show you the statement, but I don't think it's very important. I would just quote you as saying that "Major Nikolic said that he was the Chief of Staff of the Bratunac Brigade." Is that one of the positions he told you that he had?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that is one of the positions that he indicated he had, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when Major Nikolic is holding on from telling you his position, is he lying to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't confirm that, sir, because he gave me another position every time. So I did not know when he was lying or -- perhaps he changed positions often. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And looking specifically at your dealings with Major Nikolic, would it be a fair statement to say that you were not surprised that he would give you different information at different times?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not surprised by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on to a different topic. Yesterday, during your testimony - and that is on page 13, lines 19 to 21 - you mention that you had information on the weapons in the enclave to the effect that the 28th Division had some 4.000 to 4.500 small arms and mortars. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the number of 4.500 is referring to the small arms, of course, not to the mortars. But some mortars, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this information was available to you based on information gathered by DutchBat II prior to your arrival.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was all the information, that's correct, and given by DutchBat II. I don't know the source of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in May of 1995, during of course your tenure at DutchBat III, it was confirmed that you saw the ABiH or 28th Division wearing new combat uniforms.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my question to you is: In your capacity, again, as both the deputy commanding officer, DCO, the S4, and the S2 and sometimes the S3, that you knew that more weapons were coming in the enclave during your tenure, during the time DutchBat III was there.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the idea, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in January 1995, when you were -- again, I refer to yesterday's testimony, when you were trying to tackle the problem of freedom of movement, you confirmed that you attempted to go into the Bandera Triangle. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that at one time you were stopped by 45 armed men who would not let you go in to the Bandera Triangle.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, based on that experience -- well, first let me get to one more point, because yesterday, from your testimony, I wasn't sure if there were two incidents or one incident, because you also say - and that's on lines 13 to 20, at page 17 - "patrols were stopped as well and then ended in a blockade. For a couple of days we had to stay in the area."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you give us a bit more information about those events.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan was that altogether five patrols would enter the Bandera Triangle. I was leading the first patrol to go in. And depending on the result of that patrol, the other ones would start. I was about 2 K -- sorry, 2 kilometres within the Bandera Triangle when my patrol was stopped. The others also entered and were stopped as well. So it's the same action.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you were held back for almost two days before you could return to your --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recollect, it was about four days, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my first question in respect to this episode is that the people who stopped you, those 45 armed men, did they appear to you as acting on their own initiative, or this was organised action?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the local brigade commander, Mr. Zulfo, was present. He was the one that stopped me in person, and he was backed up by those, about, 40 men. So it was not on his -- at least not on the initiative of those men; probably on the initiative of Mr. Zulfo, being the brigade commander of the BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I just want to make sure that the transcript reflects what he says. Was it Mr. Zulfo himself the one that stopped you in person or -- it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was, backed up by those 40 men, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to make sure that you said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, at least for this single incident, you would agree with me that what you were dealing with was an organised army.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For this single incident, yes, correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my second question with respect to this incident is: In the end, you could never see what was in the Bandera Triangle.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And even though you don't know, there could have been a complete army in that triangle. There was enough room there for such, but you don't know.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we could -- we have insight in about, let's say, 50 per cent of the area, because in that area we had some higher ground. But we couldn't -- a hell of a lot could be concealed over there; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And we're talking about an area that, you know, realistically speaking, is a good 5 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 5 or 2 kilometres, yes, and going to a point, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because you have used the word "army" twice; once in what I would describe as a microscopic context and the other one in a macroscopic context. I would like to know what the witness understands by "army." What would you understand an army to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An army is a military organisation with command lines, and recognisable as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you answered the question that was put to you by Mr. Bourgon minutes ago -- yes, at line 20 the question was: "Now, at least for this single incident, you would agree with me that what you were dealing with was an organised army." And you answered: "For this single incident, yes, correct, sir." So could you now quantify, explain, why, having met this first batch of about 40 persons with this certain Zulfo stopping you, you came to the conclusion or you come to the conclusion today that you were dealing, for that single incident, with an organised army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My remark concerning the single incident, sir, is because later on the organisation was not that obvious. And on the very moment in that incident, it is loud and clear that the men acting, the 40 men, were under command and following orders or guidelines of Mr. Zulfo. So that led me to a conclusion that I had -- I coped with an army unit. My exception for this incident refers to the, let's say, undisciplined way we were confronted later on with, so more or less incorrect. But for this occasion, on that moment, it was clearly an organised military unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, just to clarify the second question about what you could not see within the Bandera Triangle, I indicated to you there could have been a complete army. Let me rephrase this question. There could have been many more soldiers and many more weapons that you never had a chance to see?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me move on to a different topic, and that is the taking of observation post Echo, or OP Echo. Before I get into this topic, I would just like to confirm with you that, during your tenure with DutchBat III, you did not have access, nor did you see any of the internal documents, such as orders, operational orders, or reports, within the VRS.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I certainly did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You did not have access to such documentation.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have access, neither did I see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So when you drew conclusions about actions taken by the VRS, you could only do that on the basis of your experience and what you saw on the ground.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when OP Echo was taken - and I refer to your testimony yesterday on page 30, line 25, and page 31, lines 1 to 8 - when OP Echo was taken, you first thought that this was the beginning of a major attack on the enclave, but then you realised that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in the end you concluded that this was one or both of the above, which is a test case or, more importantly, to get control of the road for the BSA to improve their east-to-west connections.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the aim in this particular incident, at the end you concluded that this was the case; but you never were informed of what the aim of the Bosnian Serb army was in taking these actions.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That was our own conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll move to a different topic. You are familiar, sir, with the term "rules of engagement"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I'd like you to confirm, even though this was not discussed but it was discussed indirectly, that your rules of engagement were United Nations rules of engagement, and that the use of force for DutchBat III was limited to self-defence.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And "self-defence," if you clarify for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, means, unless a member of DutchBat is attacked, you cannot use deadly force.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you gave that green order to B Company on 10 July, then self-defence went down the drain and now you had to act, as you said yesterday, as a real army.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So from that point on, would you agree with me that, in fact, you were now [Realtime transcript read in error "not"] engaged in an armed confrontation with the BSA.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: With the Serb army. That from that point on, from the moment that order, the green order, was given --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- you were in an armed confrontation with --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, yes, because I read here "you were not engaged," but I was engaged. That's why I stopped, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Probably my mistake, Mr. President. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There's an error in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, of course, you would agree with me also that once you fire back on the Serb army, or any army, this is likely to cause a reaction, that this army will now treat you as hostile and now use force on you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to the ultimatum that you received from the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
